blocks.text: A lumbar puncture (LP) set is a collection of sterile instruments and consumables used to access the subarachnoid space in the lumbar region of the vertebral column to obtain cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), measure CSF opening pressure, or administer selected intrathecal medications.
It is used in the investigation of conditions such as meningitis, encephalitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage in selected cases, inflammatory neurological diseases and certain malignancies.
The procedure is usually performed below the termination of the spinal cord, commonly at the L3–L4 or L4–L5 intervertebral space in adults.
OSCE identification statement:

“This is a lumbar puncture set, used to access the lumbar subarachnoid space for cerebrospinal fluid sampling, measurement of opening pressure and, in selected circumstances, administration of intrathecal medication.”
A lumbar puncture set may contain a spinal needle, introducer, stylet, manometer and collection tubes. The exact contents vary between manufacturers and procedures.

content_groups.group_title: Important parts of the spinal needle

blocks.text: mannersmedical.com

items.text: Hub: The proximal part used to hold the needle and attach compatible connectors.
Shaft: The long, hollow portion of the needle.
Bevel or pencil-point tip: The distal end that penetrates tissue; the design varies by needle type.
Lumen: The internal channel through which CSF flows.
Stylet: The removable inner component that occupies the lumen during insertion.

blocks.text: OSCE tip: Do not confuse the stylet with the spinal needle. The stylet is removed once the needle is appropriately positioned, according to the procedural technique.
A. Quincke needle
A cutting needle with a bevelled tip.

items.text: Commonly used for diagnostic lumbar puncture.
Allows CSF flow after the stylet is removed.
May be associated with a higher risk of post-dural puncture headache than atraumatic needles.

blocks.text: B. Whitacre needle
An atraumatic pencil-point needle with a lateral opening.

items.text: Separates rather than cutting dural fibres in the same way as a cutting bevel.
Commonly used with an introducer.
Associated with a lower risk of post-dural puncture headache.

blocks.text: C. Sprotte needle
Another atraumatic pencil-point needle with a lateral opening.

items.text: Designed to reduce dural trauma.
Used for diagnostic LP and other appropriate spinal procedures.

blocks.text: Spinal needles vary in gauge and length according to patient size, anatomy and procedural requirements. Needles around 22–25G are commonly encountered in diagnostic LP practice.
Remember: a higher gauge number indicates a smaller needle diameter.

items.text: Needle tip: Cutting or atraumatic.
Needle construction: With or without a separate introducer.
Pressure measurement: Sets with or without a manometer.
Procedure: Diagnostic lumbar puncture, therapeutic CSF removal, or specialised intrathecal procedures.
Patient group: Adult, paediatric or neonatal equipment, selected according to patient anatomy and clinical needs.

blocks.text: A lumbar puncture set is not necessarily a complete spinal anaesthesia kit, although some components overlap.
The principle is to introduce a sterile spinal needle into the lumbar subarachnoid space, which contains CSF.
Once the needle is correctly positioned and the stylet is removed, CSF may flow through the needle lumen. The fluid is collected into sterile tubes for analysis.
If indicated, opening pressure is measured with the patient appropriately positioned and the pressure-measuring system correctly connected.
The procedure requires strict aseptic technique and careful assessment for contraindications.

items.text: Suspected meningitis, including bacterial, viral or fungal infection.
Suspected encephalitis when CSF investigation is appropriate.
Investigation of inflammatory neurological disorders, such as multiple sclerosis or Guillain–Barré syndrome.
Suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage when further investigation is indicated after initial assessment.
Investigation of selected neurological malignancies.
Measurement of CSF opening pressure in appropriate clinical circumstances.
Selected diagnostic tests for neurological infections or inflammatory disease.
Therapeutic CSF drainage in selected conditions under specialist guidance.
Intrathecal administration of certain medications, such as selected chemotherapy agents, when specifically indicated and performed using the appropriate protocol.

blocks.text: Important: CSF removal is not a routine treatment for every cause of raised intracranial pressure. The underlying condition and risk of dangerous pressure gradients must be assessed first.

The spinal cord in most adults terminates around the L1–L2 vertebral level. Therefore, lumbar puncture is usually performed below this level.
The line joining the highest points of the iliac crests approximates the L4 vertebral level or L4–L5 interspace, although this landmark is not perfectly reliable.
Lateral decubitus
The patient lies on their side with the back flexed. This position is preferred when measuring opening pressure.
Sitting position
The patient sits leaning forward to widen the intervertebral spaces. This can facilitate needle insertion but is not the standard position for a reliable opening pressure measurement.
The following is a structured overview for examination purposes. Actual performance requires supervised clinical training and adherence to local protocols.

items.text: Confirm patient identity and the clinical indication.
Explain the procedure and obtain informed consent.
Review relevant history, medications, coagulation status and neurological findings.
Assess for contraindications, including suspected mass effect or unsafe intracranial pressure gradients.
Gather equipment and prepare the sterile field.
Position the patient appropriately.
Perform hand hygiene and wear appropriate protective equipment.
Clean the puncture site with an appropriate antiseptic.
Allow the antiseptic to dry according to the product instructions.
Apply sterile drapes and use sterile gloves.
Administer local anaesthetic where indicated.
Identify the appropriate lumbar interspace.
Insert the spinal needle using the appropriate technique for the selected needle.
Advance carefully, observing for expected changes in resistance.
Remove the stylet according to the procedural technique to assess for CSF return.
If CSF does not appear, reassess needle position rather than applying force.

blocks.text: When clinically indicated, measure opening pressure before collecting substantial volumes of CSF.

items.text: The patient should be in the lateral decubitus position.
The patient should be relaxed, with the pressure-measuring system properly connected.
Record the pressure and units, commonly cm H₂O.
Avoid interpreting a reading without considering positioning, patient effort, ventilation and the clinical context.
Allow CSF to drip into the appropriate sterile tubes.
Avoid routine forceful aspiration.
Collect the required volume according to the requested tests and local protocol.
Label each tube accurately and send specimens promptly.
Replace the stylet before withdrawing the needle when required by the needle design and local technique.
Withdraw the needle and apply a small sterile dressing.
Document the procedure, opening pressure if measured, CSF appearance, specimen collection and any complications.
Provide appropriate post-procedure advice and monitor the patient.

Commonly around 6–25 cm H₂O in adults, depending on context and measurement conditions

blocks.text: These values are approximate. Reference intervals differ by laboratory, age and clinical circumstances.
A key OSCE question is when a lumbar puncture should be delayed or avoided.

content_groups.group_title: Important contraindications or reasons to defer

items.text: Suspected intracranial mass effect or a dangerous pressure gradient, particularly with clinical evidence of impending herniation.
Infection at the intended puncture site.
Significant uncorrected coagulopathy or clinically important bleeding risk.
Severe cardiorespiratory or haemodynamic instability that makes the procedure unsafe.
Suspected spinal anatomy or pathology that makes the intended approach unsafe.

content_groups.group_title: When imaging may be required first

blocks.text: Neuroimaging is not mandatory before every lumbar puncture. It is considered when clinical features raise concern for mass effect or another intracranial condition that could make LP unsafe.

Concerning features may include focal neurological deficits, papilloedema, significantly impaired consciousness, new seizures or relevant immunocompromise, depending on the overall presentation and local guidelines.

Critical emergency point: If bacterial meningitis is suspected and LP is unsafe or would significantly delay treatment, obtain blood cultures when feasible and start appropriate empirical antimicrobial treatment promptly. Do not delay lifesaving treatment while waiting for imaging or LP.
1. Post-dural puncture headache
A characteristic headache that often worsens when upright and improves when lying down. Atraumatic needles reduce its incidence.
2. Back pain and local tenderness
Usually mild and temporary.
3. Bleeding or spinal haematoma
Rare but potentially serious, especially with coagulation abnormalities or antithrombotic medication.
4. Cerebral herniation
A catastrophic complication in patients with certain intracranial mass lesions or dangerous pressure gradients. Appropriate pre-procedure assessment is essential.
5. Nerve root irritation
May produce transient shooting pain or paraesthesia during needle placement. Persistent neurological symptoms require urgent assessment.
Other possible complications include infection, a traumatic tap, failed or repeated attempts, and CSF leakage.
Routine prolonged bed rest has not been shown to prevent post-dural puncture headache.
Advantages

items.text: Provides direct access to CSF for diagnosis.
Can identify potentially life-threatening infections.
Enables measurement of opening pressure.
Allows selected therapeutic interventions.
Can be performed at the bedside without general anaesthesia in many patients.

blocks.text: Disadvantages

items.text: Requires appropriate training and aseptic technique.
May be technically difficult in obesity, spinal deformity or certain anatomical conditions.
Can cause headache, discomfort or bleeding.
Results may be affected by a traumatic tap.
May be unsafe in certain intracranial or coagulation conditions.
Some investigations require rapid specimen transport and specialised laboratory processing.

blocks.text: Q1. Identify the instrument.
A lumbar puncture set used to access the lumbar subarachnoid space for CSF collection, pressure measurement and selected intrathecal procedures.
Q2. At which vertebral levels is LP commonly performed in adults?
L3–L4 or L4–L5, below the usual termination of the spinal cord.
Q3. What is the function of the stylet?
It occupies the needle lumen during insertion, helping prevent tissue coring and obstruction.
Q4. What is the difference between a Quincke and a Whitacre needle?
Quincke is a cutting-bevel needle; Whitacre is an atraumatic pencil-point needle with a lateral opening.
Q5. Which position is preferred for measuring opening pressure?
The lateral decubitus position, with the patient relaxed and the measurement system properly positioned.
Q6. What is the most characteristic complication?
Post-dural puncture headache.
Q7. Name four CSF investigations.
Cell count and differential, protein, glucose, and microbiological studies such as Gram stain and culture.
Q8. What is the major contraindication tested in OSCEs?
Suspected intracranial mass effect or a dangerous pressure gradient that could precipitate cerebral herniation.
Q9. Should antibiotics be delayed if LP cannot safely be performed immediately in suspected bacterial meningitis?
No. Start appropriate empirical treatment promptly after obtaining blood cultures when feasible.

blocks.title: Before completing the station, ensure you can:

items.text: Identify the lumbar puncture set and its components.
Label the spinal needle, stylet, hub and introducer.
Describe the difference between cutting and atraumatic needles.
Identify L3–L4 and L4–L5 as common adult puncture levels.
Explain indications, contraindications and positioning.
Describe opening-pressure measurement and CSF collection.
State normal adult CSF reference values approximately.
Recognise post-dural puncture headache, bleeding and cerebral herniation as important complications.
Explain why urgent treatment for suspected bacterial meningitis must not be delayed when LP is unsafe.
Site: Usually L3–L4 or L4–L5 in adults.
Position for opening pressure: Lateral decubitus.
Characteristic complication: Post-dural puncture headache, less frequent with atraumatic needles.
